claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr can form a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial high-temperature HfNbTaTiZr solid solution has negligible chemical short-range order.
BCC refractory high-entropy alloys can have a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering.
Intermediate-temperature isothermal annealing can evolve SRO from isolated clusters into a percolating network.
Such annealing can produce a percolating SRO network while preserving a single-phase BCC structure.
Annealing between 0.4 Tm and 0.7 Tm is an appropriate regime for driving the proposed SRO evolution.
Quenching to room temperature preserves the high-temperature SRO configuration for subsequent measurement.
A critical SRO volume fraction and spatial connectivity produce a percolative transition.
The percolating SRO network creates low-thermal-conductivity pathways.
Percolating SRO causes a nonlinear, super-additive reduction in lattice thermal conductivity that exceeds standard scattering-model predictions.
Chemically ordered domains disrupt phonon mean free paths through coherent-interface scattering.
Mass-difference fluctuations associated with SRO provide scattering distinct from isolated point-defect scattering.
SRO domains have a vibrational density of states distinct from that of the surrounding matrix.
Connectivity of regions with distinct vibrational density of states forms a percolative barrier to phonon transport.
Lattice thermal conductivity drops sharply when the SRO connectivity threshold is crossed.
After the threshold-associated conductivity drop, lattice thermal conductivity reaches a plateau or declines more slowly.
Debye-Callaway and serial/parallel effective-medium models predict a linear or sub-linear conductivity decrease with increasing SRO concentration.
The proposed mechanism requires SRO clusters to alter local force constants significantly without causing an ordered-intermetallic or crystal-structure transformation.
The percolation threshold depends on pair-interaction energies and SRO-evolution kinetics.
Anharmonic effects may influence the measured conductivity drop and may be difficult to separate from percolative scattering.
